result.summary: Pausanias calls the Argive war on Thebes the most memorable war between Greeks of the heroic age. He describes the first expedition under Adrastus, which was destroyed, and the later expedition of the Epigoni under Thersander, which took Thebes. He ends with a note on the epic Thebais and its authorship.

scenes.title: Adrastus' Army Defeated at Thebes
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains why the war was so notable, then tells how Adrastus' allied army was beaten at Ismenius and by sallies from the walls. Only Adrastus survived, and the costly Theban win gave rise to the phrase Cadmean victory.
scenes.stakes: The Argive army risks destruction; the Thebans risk losing their city.

scenes.title: The Epigoni Take Thebes
scenes.summary: The Epigoni march against Thebes with Thersander. After a hard battle at Glisas, the Thebans are beaten; some flee with Laodamas and the rest are reduced by blockade.
scenes.stakes: The Thebans risk defeat, exile and capture of their city.

scenes.title: The Thebais and Its Author
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes that the epic Thebais concerns this war. Callinus attributed it to Homer, but Pausanias thinks it later than the Iliad and Odyssey.

notable_quotes.reason: Gives the origin of the phrase Cadmean victory, a win with heavy loss.

analysis.text: Pausanias treats the Theban wars as historical events, judging them by scale, cost and consequence among Greek wars.
His discussion of the Thebais shows ancient literary scholarship, with competing views on Homer's authorship and a critic's judgment about date.

legacy.text: The phrase Cadmean victory, a win bringing ruinous loss, is the ancestor of the later expression Pyrrhic victory.

fun_facts.text: The Thebais is lost; only fragments survive, though it was once ranked among the Epic Cycle poems.

language_notes.text: The war of the Seven against Thebes, fought by Adrastus of Argos to restore Polynices to the Theban throne against his brother Eteocles.
Earlier local wars: Eleusis against Athens, and Thebes against the Minyæ of Orchomenus. Pausanias says each ended after a single engagement.
Phlegyæ: a warlike people associated with the Minyan region of Orchomenus, here fighting as allies of Thebes.
A Cadmean victory is a win as ruinous as a defeat. Cadmus was Thebes' legendary founder, so the Thebans are called Cadmeans.
Epigoni means 'those born afterwards': the sons of the Seven, who attacked Thebes a generation later to avenge their fathers.
Callinus was an early Greek elegiac poet of Ephesus who cited the Thebais as Homer's work.

context_notes.text: Ismenius is the area by the river Ismenus and the sanctuary of Apollo Ismenius near Thebes.
Glisas was a place near Thebes, on the road toward Chalcis, where the Epigoni's decisive battle was said to have taken place.
Œdipus' sons Eteocles and Polynices quarrelled over the rule of Thebes, which caused the war.

literary_notes.text: The invaders attack with zeal but lack siegecraft, so their eagerness destroys them. Adrastus alone survives, a bleak outcome.
Pausanias speaks in the first person as a critical scholar, weighing earlier authorities and offering his own judgment on the poem's date.
